agree.reason: The partner gets a clear, competent case and an open account of the March error, but nothing shows the fix has worked or what she would commit to as a supervisor, so a doubtful reader has little reason to approve now rather than wait.

honest.reason: Every figure matches the brief, but 'I'm already doing much of that work' turns training three new hires into supervision, which claims more than the facts support.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out that she billed 90 hours over target, but it leaves out the strongest available number (no wrong or missed deadlines in about 600 entries since April) and never shows the size of the case and trial load.

right_comparison.reason: It never compares what the group gets if she is promoted against keeping things as they are, or against someone else doing the supervising and owning the deadline sheet.

qualification.reason: A reader with doubts about her reliability needs checkable commitments, such as certification by June or weekly check-ins, but the letter offers no dated or measurable commitment at all.

objections.reason: It raises the March error directly and owns it, but it answers with the process change alone and gives no evidence that the change has worked, so the partner's concern is only partly answered.

fit.reason: It is a well-organized letter well under 400 words, but it leaves name placeholders and asks to 'discuss' instead of requesting the in-person meeting before the December 15 deadline.
